issues.legal_issue: A factual objection that a participant could not belong to the family cannot be accepted on appeal when it was not raised or supported in the proceedings below.
material_facts: The appellant argued on appeal that the plaintiff, as a uterine brother, could not be a member of the family involved in the arrangement.
The appellant had not raised that contention in the written statement, no issue had been framed on it, and the record contained no supporting evidence.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to accept the contention that the plaintiff could not have been a member of the family merely because he was the appellant’s uterine brother.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the absence of a specific plea, an issue, and evidence supporting the factual contention; it cited no provision or earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.civil_property_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a civil dispute about property.
predicates.new_family_membership_objection: A party raises on appeal a factual objection that another participant could not belong to the relevant family.
predicates.no_pleading_issue_or_evidence: The objection was not specifically pleaded below, no issue was framed on it, and the record contains no supporting evidence.

issues.definition: When a party raises a family-membership objection for the first time on appeal without a supporting plea, issue, or evidence, the appellate court declines to accept it.

issues.legal_issue: A family arrangement may be established by an oral agreement recorded in a writing, and the absence of a family member’s written statement does not invalidate the arrangement where that member consented to it.
material_facts: The parties asserted competing claims to the properties, with the appellant claiming that the properties were his self-acquired property and the plaintiff claiming a share.
A document recorded the brothers’ statements and their agreement about the properties and their enjoyment.
The plaintiff alleged and testified that their mother consented to the arrangement and was to retain and enjoy a house property, although her statement was not recorded in the document.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the finding that the parties had made a family arrangement and that the document recorded it; the mother’s consent did not have to be recorded in the document.
issues.legal_principle: A family arrangement may be made orally, and a writing may simply record what has already been agreed. The Court also relied on Sahu Madho Das v. Mukhand Ram in explaining the treatment of antecedent claims in family arrangements.

rule.if: civil_property_partition_dispute and competing_property_claims and arrangement_resolves_claims and oral_family_agreement and family_member_consented

predicates.civil_property_partition_dispute: The proceeding concerns a claim to divide or obtain possession of property among persons asserting family-related rights.
predicates.competing_property_claims: The participants assert competing claims concerning rights in the property.
predicates.arrangement_resolves_claims: The participants agree how the disputed property or its enjoyment will be allocated among them.
predicates.oral_family_agreement: The arrangement was agreed orally, even if its terms were later recorded in writing.
predicates.family_member_consented: A family member whose interests were addressed by the arrangement consented to it, even though that member’s statement was not written into the record.

issues.definition: When competing property claims in a family property dispute are resolved by an oral arrangement to which the affected family member consented, the arrangement is valid even if a writing does not record that member’s statement.

issues.legal_issue: A family arrangement does not require proof that the participants actually held antecedent title where they asserted claims to rights and the arrangement recognized those claims rather than treating one participant as the sole owner transferring property to the others.
material_facts: The appellant claimed that the properties were his self-acquired property, while the plaintiff claimed a share in them.

Evidence indicated that the landed property had been purchased with the mother’s money, but the document treated the property as joint property of the three brothers and did not recognize any brother as its sole owner.
The arrangement allocated rights and enjoyment among the brothers rather than recording a transfer from a recognized sole owner.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that actual antecedent title did not have to be established; a claim to such a right was sufficient in the circumstances, and the arrangement did not operate as a transfer by a sole owner.
issues.legal_principle: The Court explained Sahu Madho Das v. Mukhand Ram as allowing the parties’ antecedent title to be assumed and defined by their arrangement; it distinguished a case in which others receive property by transfer from a participant whose sole ownership they recognize.

rule.if: family_property_arrangement_dispute and participants_assert_antecedent_rights and arrangement_recognizes_shared_claims and no_sole_owner_transfer

predicates.family_property_arrangement_dispute: The proceeding concerns an arrangement among family participants about rights in property.
predicates.participants_assert_antecedent_rights: The participants assert claims to rights in the property predating or underlying the arrangement.
predicates.arrangement_recognizes_shared_claims: The arrangement recognizes or defines the participants’ competing or shared claims rather than treating one as the sole owner.
predicates.no_sole_owner_transfer: The arrangement does not recognize one participant as sole owner and provide for that participant to transfer property to the others.

issues.definition: Where family participants assert antecedent rights and their arrangement defines shared claims without a transfer from a recognized sole owner, those rights need not be proved as actual title.

issues.legal_issue: A writing recording a family arrangement does not require compulsory registration when it merely memorializes an arrangement already made and is not itself the instrument that creates or declares the parties’ rights.
material_facts: The document recorded the brothers’ statements and said that they had agreed to those statements and kept copies as proof.
The Court found that the document recorded what had already been decided and was evidence of the arrangement, not the basis of the parties’ rights in the property.
The document did not recognize any brother as sole owner transferring property to the others.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the document was a memorandum of the arrangement and did not require compulsory registration under Section 17 of the Indian Registration Act.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 17 of the Indian Registration Act, compulsory registration applies when the writing itself brings about the arrangement or declares rights in property for future use as a document of title. A writing that only records a prior oral arrangement as evidence does not require compulsory registration.

rule.if: family_property_arrangement_dispute and writing_records_prior_agreement and writing_is_evidence_only and writing_does_not_create_or_declare_property_rights

predicates.family_property_arrangement_dispute: The proceeding concerns an arrangement about rights in family property.
predicates.writing_records_prior_agreement: The participants made the arrangement before the writing was prepared, and the writing records what they had agreed.
predicates.writing_is_evidence_only: The writing serves as proof or a record of the prior arrangement rather than as the operative instrument of agreement.
predicates.writing_does_not_create_or_declare_prope: The writing itself does not create or declare the participants’ property rights for the future.

issues.definition: A writing in a family property dispute is not compulsorily registrable when it only evidences a prior agreement and does not itself create or declare property rights.
